description: The single source of truth for every numeric budget the console is gated on. Rows carry a `scope`. A `product` row is one of `Spec-023 §Console Design (Meridian)` §Budgets' own figures: every budget that table names appears here exactly once, whether or not this revision can measure it, because a budget silently omitted is a budget nobody notices is ungated. A `harness` row is a bound the test scaffolding itself applies — no spec figure stands behind it, so its `specTarget` states the bound in its own terms while `harnessBudgetDerivation` states, once for the whole set, why those figures and not others. Both kinds live here for the same reason: one value, one home. An entry whose `status` is "n/a" is not measurable at this revision and names, in `producedBy`, the Plan-023 task that makes it measurable and, in `notMeasurableReason`, what is missing. Every harness that reads this file prints one line per "n/a" entry beside the budgets it did measure.
harnessBudgetDerivation: The five `console-*` harness rows are the slices of ONE tier timeout, so their derivation is a property of the set and is stated here rather than five times over. Three of them bound the launch: `launch-deadline.ts` mints a single deadline per launch and divides it into readiness, the frame witness, and cleanup, so a launch that overruns produces its own diagnostic instead of vitest's undiagnosable kill. The other two bound what runs BETWEEN a settled launch and its cleanup — the caller's test body, which was budgeted by nothing until 2026-09-05 and could therefore be killed by vitest mid-poll, before the poll's own message or the cleanup settled, leaving an Electron alive. A launching tier's `testTimeout` is now DERIVED from these rows rather than written as a literal: `tierTimeoutFor()` in `launch-deadline.ts` sums the launch budget, the body allowance that tier applies, and a 2 000 ms settlement residual — a floor rather than a ceiling, which is why it is a constant beside those rows and not a row among them, since every row here is a ceiling. `architecture/launch-deadline.test.ts` resolves every launching tier through `createVitest` and holds its real `testTimeout` and `hookTimeout` against those derived figures, never against a literal copied out of the config. The body allowance is per tier because the two tiers' bodies are different subjects — a driven interaction against a sustained workload — and a tier that states none gets the shorter one, so a new tier fails loudly inside its own bound rather than quietly under vitest's. The figures are generous on purpose: a cold CI runner with no warm Electron cache is the case these must not flake on, and each is a ceiling for a wedged phase rather than an expectation.

unitConventions.kB: 1000 bytes (SI). The spec writes `kB`; the SI reading is also the stricter one (450 kB = 450000 B, against 450 KiB = 460800 B), so taking it costs the budget nothing and cannot make a passing measurement out of a failing one.
unitConventions.MB: 1000000 bytes (SI), by the same reading and the same reasoning (120 MB = 120000000 B, against 120 MiB = 125829120 B).
unitConventions.MiB: 1048576 bytes (binary). The spec writes `MiB` for the terminal budget explicitly, so this one is not an interpretation.
unitConventions.percentOfOneCore: percent of a single core, averaged over the window the budget's `specTarget` names

measurementProtocol.deterministic: Bundle size, heap at rest, steady heap, and first-ledger-row latency against the fixture's frozen clock gate on any runner (Spec-023 §Budgets, "Where they are measured").
measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent: Frame time and CPU are measured from the built bundle in the Electron shell against the fixture bridge's flagship scenario with the frozen clock, ten warm-up seconds discarded, the metric taken as the median of three runs, on the pinned CI runner class the desktop workflow names by label, with thresholds calibrated on that class at first landing with 25 % headroom and one automatic re-run before a failure counts.
measurementProtocol.referenceProfile: The `limit` figures are the product targets on the laptop-class reference profile — eight cores, integrated GPU, one 60 Hz display — which the endurance ledger records beside the runner-calibrated thresholds so a runner regression and a product regression stay distinguishable.

budgets.label: Renderer initial bundle
budgets.subject: The gzip-compressed byte total of every asset in the renderer entry document's initial import graph under `apps/desktop/out/renderer` — the entry module scripts, the `modulepreload` graph, the entry stylesheets, and every chunk reachable from them by a static import — excluding lazy chunks (terminal, node graph, math, diagrams, browser tools), excluding source maps, and excluding the entry HTML document itself.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 450 kB gzip, excluding lazy chunks (terminal, node graph, math, diagrams, browser tools)
budgets.notes: Gated on gzip because the spec's figure is a gzip figure. Brotli is measured and reported for every asset beside it — it is what the renderer protocol handler can actually serve — but it is reported, never gated, so the gate and the spec agree byte for byte. CI enforcement of this gate is T-023p-1C-8's leg; the measurement and its budget row land here.

budgets.label: Frame time, four lanes streaming
budgets.subject: The 95th-percentile frame duration of the renderer while four agent lanes stream concurrently into the ledger, measured from the built bundle in the Electron shell against the fixture bridge's flagship scenario with the frozen clock.
budgets.specTarget: p95 ≤ 16.7 ms on the reference machine
budgets.notMeasurableReason: There is no four-lane streaming scenario to measure. The flagship scenario, the ledger frame, the reveal engine, and the cast bar are T-023p-1C-2's; until they land there is no render path whose frames could be sampled, and a synthetic stand-in would measure the harness rather than the console.
budgets.notes: Hardware-dependent: gates on the pinned CI runner class only, per `measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent`.

budgets.label: Renderer heap, one session open at rest
budgets.subject: Retained JavaScript heap with one session open and nothing streaming — the console's stores, projections, and persistence layer settled, after a forced garbage collection.
budgets.notes: Deliberately NOT measured in a Node process. Until 2026-09-02 this row was `enforced` against `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` in the budget CLI with a stand-in entity map retained — no Chromium, no renderer isolate, no React, no DOM, no console store — so the gate could report green over a renderer well past 120 MB, which is the one failure a budget exists to catch. It was then recorded `n/a` rather than re-pointed, because the subject was out of reach: nothing delivered events into a session store, so the only reading available was a renderer with an EMPTY session open. The fixture bridge now serves the growth port's session read and the scenario engine drives beats through the apply chokepoint into it, so the subject exists and the row is gated again — on the endurance tier, which launches the built console, opens the flagship scenario's own session, walks the frozen clock over the whole script, asserts the store admitted events through a live subscription, and reads `performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize` as the minimum over settling samples. That figure counts allocated-and-not-yet-collected bytes, so it sits at or above the retained heap this row bounds, which is the safe direction for a ceiling. The reading is a renderer isolate figure taken in the Electron shell in unobtrusive-window mode; the substrate floor recorded on 2026-09-02 with no session content was 6,564,912 B.

budgets.label: Steady heap, flagship replay
budgets.subject: Renderer heap over a thirty-minute flagship replay — both its ceiling and its slope, since a heap that stays under the ceiling while climbing monotonically is still a leak.
budgets.specTarget: flat over thirty minutes; ≤ 250 MB renderer heap
additionalCriteria: The heap is flat over the thirty-minute replay: no monotonic growth across the run's snapshot series.
budgets.notMeasurableReason: The endurance tier does not exist: no thirty-minute flagship replay, no CDP heap-snapshot helper, and no dated endurance ledger to record refutations in. The scenario it replays is additionally T-023p-1C-2's.
budgets.notes: `Spec-023 §Console Test Tiers` places this on the endurance tier — heap snapshots captured by an own CDP helper, analyzed with memlab, results in a dated ledger.

budgets.label: Idle CPU, session open, nothing streaming
budgets.subject: CPU consumed by the renderer with a session open and no stream running, averaged over sixty seconds — together with the assertion that no timer fires in that window except the refresh scheduler's deadline and the presence heartbeat.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 0.5 % of one core averaged over sixty seconds; no timer fires except the refresh scheduler's deadline and the presence heartbeat
additionalCriteria: No timer fires during the sixty-second window except the refresh scheduler's absolute deadline and the presence heartbeat.
budgets.notMeasurableReason: There is no session surface to open and no scheduler whose timers could be enumerated; the measurement runs the built bundle in the Electron shell against the flagship scenario (T-023p-1C-2) and is taken by the endurance reference run (T-023p-1C-8).
budgets.notes: Hardware-dependent: gates on the pinned CI runner class only, per `measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent`. The timer-enumeration half is a tripwire on the architecture tier, not a number.

budgets.label: Streaming CPU, one lane
budgets.subject: CPU consumed by the renderer while one agent lane streams into the ledger, together with the assertion that the reveal engine yields when the frame budget is spent rather than overrunning it.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 15 % of one core on the reference machine; the reveal engine yields when the frame budget is spent
additionalCriteria: The reveal engine yields when the frame budget is spent.
budgets.notMeasurableReason: There is no reveal engine and no streaming lane. Both are T-023p-1C-2's; the measurement itself is the endurance reference run's at T-023p-1C-8.
budgets.notes: Hardware-dependent: gates on the pinned CI runner class only, per `measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent`.

budgets.label: Terminal instance
budgets.subject: Retained memory of one `terminal` pane instance at the default scrollback — the `@xterm/xterm` instance, its WebGL renderer, and the pane's own state.
budgets.notes: The row was `enforced` for one day, 2026-09-02, against a harness that constructed `XtermTerminalAdapter` directly under happy-dom and sampled the Node process's own heap — a subject narrower than this row's own sentence, which can report green over a pane well past the ceiling — and it was then recorded `n/a` rather than re-pointed, because no deck mounted panes and there was nothing whole to hold. It is gated again from the endurance tier, which now has one: `console/frame/PaneHarnessSurface.tsx` is a `define`-gated fixture surface, reached at `#/pane-harness/<paneKind>/<sessionId>`, that resolves the body through the deck's own `ConsolePaneRegistry` and mounts one more instance per press. So the subject is held WHOLE — the built console in a real Electron window, a `terminal` pane the registry resolved, mounted through a real React commit, its emulator on a live WebGL2 context, bound to a session the scenario engine has delivered into — and each of those is asserted rather than assumed: the run FAILS on a `dom` renderer reading rather than measuring the fallback, and fails on an empty session store rather than folding a lease off an empty log. WHAT THE HARNESS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT HOLD is the deck: no tab strip, no layout, no drag target, no detach path. That is closer to this row's sentence than a deck-mounted reading would be — the ceiling is per INSTANCE, and a figure taken inside a deck would fold the deck's own cost into it and report a pane over budget for chrome the row does not name. The figure is the difference between the settled renderer heap with no instance open and with one, taken as the minimum over settling samples, after a warm-up cycle that moves the emulator chunk's one-time cost to the left of the baseline; two further instances are then opened and their per-instance slope is required to agree with that figure, which is the control against a fixed cost being reported as the instance. The adapter-level claims that ARE reachable in a Node process — scrollback eviction, disposal, and a working day of pane churn — stay on `terminal-endurance.test.ts` beside the churn accounting they belong with; that file makes NO ceiling claim of its own, so neither half of the instance ever receives an independent allowance. WHAT THE FIGURE COVERS: the instance is priced as ONE populated pane — the mounted pane's standing cost plus a full buffer at the default scrollback, both measured at one width (`TERMINAL_BUDGET_MEASUREMENT_COLUMNS`) and one depth (`TERMINAL_DEFAULT_SCROLLBACK_LINES`, both in the cap home) and summed before a single `evaluateBudget` call. Measured 2026-09-04 on macOS: 16,456 kB of 20,480 kB (80.4 %) — pane 940 kB plus scrollback 15,516 kB at 10,000 lines × 120 columns; later panes 823 kB each; 417 kB still held after three closed; a second run reproduced the sum within 10 kB. That headroom is thin on purpose: the next thing that grows a terminal pane moves this figure, and changing either cap-home constant changes what the row means. WHAT IT CANNOT YET: the scrollback half is still driven in the driver process, because the byte stream, the scrollback, and the resize report are `Plan-023 §Console growth slate` row 3 and no wire in this revision can put a line into a MOUNTED pane — so the sum is conservative (it omits nothing the mounted pane holds and adds the buffer the pane would hold), and the day row 3 lands the harness drives bytes into the mounted pane and the two halves collapse into one delta. The readings are taken behind a forced collection over a DevTools session rather than from the sampler alone: a difference of a few hundred kilobytes is decided by WHEN the collector ran, and without it this same code measured a first instance at 4,165 kB and a per-instance slope of minus 5,765 kB.

budgets.label: Time to first ledger row on launch
budgets.subject: Elapsed time from window show to the first ledger row painted, in fixture mode against the frozen clock.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 800 ms from window show, fixture mode
budgets.notMeasurableReason: There is no ledger row to paint. The ledger frame, its row primitives, and the flagship scenario the launch path replays are all T-023p-1C-2's.
budgets.notes: Deterministic against the fixture's frozen clock, so it gates on any runner once the ledger exists — it is not one of the two hardware-dependent budgets.

budgets.label: Console launch readiness ladder
budgets.subject: Wall time from `_electron.launch()` to the renderer's frame element being present — the whole cold-start ladder (first window, `load`, the frame selector) charged once between its phases rather than once each.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 30 000 ms across every readiness phase combined
budgets.notes: The whole cold-start ladder — first window, `load`, the frame selector — charged once between its phases rather than once each, which is what the four independent 30 000 ms allowances this replaced got wrong. Generous on purpose: a cold CI runner with no warm Electron cache is the case it must not flake on. The derivation these three bounds share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Measured by `architecture/launch-deadline.test.ts`, which drives the real `LaunchDeadline` this ladder draws from and holds the aggregate against every launching tier's resolved patience.

budgets.label: Console launch first-frame witness
budgets.subject: The wait, after the renderer reports ready, for the first animation frame to arrive — the reading that separates a window that painted from one that merely opened.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 15 000 ms from readiness, not from launch
budgets.notes: Armed only once readiness has landed, so a slow boot is charged to the readiness row rather than reported as a frame that never came — the flake this split was introduced to remove. What it answers is whether the window painted at all, and late is not the same as never: it fails only on never. First-frame LATENCY is bounded by nothing at this revision — `frame-time-p95-four-lanes` is the row that would catch a frame-schedule regression and it is `n/a` until T-023p-1C-2 — so a green witness is a claim about paint and never about how long the paint took. The derivation these three bounds share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Measured by the suite that drives the race rather than by the one that reads the figure: `architecture/frame-witness.test.ts` constructs the real `FrameWitness` over a source that delivers late and one that never delivers, which is the boundary this bound decides. It named `architecture/launch-deadline.test.ts` until 2026-09-05, a file that holds this figure against its constant and drives no witness at all.

budgets.label: Console launch cleanup
budgets.subject: The bound `application.close()` is raced against before the Electron process tree is SIGKILLed and the temporary profile removed.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 10 000 ms, or the tree is terminated
budgets.notes: A ceiling rather than a target: what it guards against is an Electron wedged rather than slow, so what matters is that some finite number is enforced. It is the WHOLE applied bound and the same one on both closing paths — a close reached from a failed launch is held to it exactly as one reached minutes later on the success path is, so the figure a budget audit reads is the figure the harness enforces. It was a floor until 2026-09-04, raised by whatever the launch deadline had left, which handed an early readiness failure nearly the whole 55 000 ms deadline. Because `terminated` records and passes, this figure decides when the process tree is SIGKILLed rather than whether the tier goes red; `unterminable` and `closed-after-rejection` fail, and those are the two settlements that harm the launches after them. The derivation these three bounds share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Measured by `architecture/bounded-cleanup.test.ts`, which races a real `BoundedCleanup` against a close that never settles and one that rejects; it named `architecture/launch-deadline.test.ts` until 2026-09-05, which applies this bound to nothing.

budgets.label: Console launch test-body allowance
budgets.subject: The wall time a test body gets between a settled launch and its cleanup — the interval `withLaunchedConsole` runs the caller's own function in, and the default for a tier that states no allowance of its own.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 70 000 ms between a settled launch and its cleanup
budgets.notes: Counted from the worst body in the tree rather than chosen, and RE-COUNTED on 2026-09-05 once every wait in that body was made to draw on this allowance. `e2e/frame-boot.test.ts`'s scheme-persistence case declares, in order: the palette overlay opening at 10 000 ms; three 10 000 ms `expect.poll` waits, on the applied attribute, on the durable write, and on the attribute after a reload — 30 000 ms in all; and the reload, whose navigation and the frame element it must produce share ONE 30 000 ms clock, because the renderer boot they perform between them is the same subject `console-launch-readiness` bounds. 10 000 + 30 000 + 30 000 is this figure. The 60 000 it replaces counted the polls and the reload and omitted the overlay wait, which carried Playwright's default rather than any figure written down here. A bound under a body's own declared waits would fire first and replace that body's message ("the scheme did not change") with a sentence about a clock, which is the inversion the launch deadline exists to undo. A body is handed what is LEFT of this allowance and asks for `boundedMs(<its own bound>)`, the smaller of the two, so the first wait that cannot fit fails with ITS sentence rather than the generic overrun; `architecture/body-allowance-consumption.test.ts` reads both launching tiers and fails a bounded wait that names no allowance. The derivation these rows share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`.

budgets.label: Console endurance test-body allowance
budgets.subject: The wall time the endurance tier's sustained workload gets between a settled launch and its cleanup — hundreds of driven churn cycles and the settling heap samples either side of them.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 540 000 ms between a settled launch and its cleanup
budgets.notes: A separate figure because the endurance body is a different subject from an end-to-end one, not a slower version of it: `steady-state.test.ts` drives 200 churn cycles twice over with settling heap samples either side, which its own count comment measures at roughly 50 ms a cycle — well under a minute warm, and the reason that tier has always carried a patience an order of magnitude past the end-to-end one. Nine minutes keeps the derived tier timeout at the 597 000 ms this tier effectively had before the arithmetic was made explicit, so nothing about a tier nobody has complained about is tightened here. Its own waits draw on this allowance through the same `boundedMs` the end-to-end bodies use, but this FIGURE is deliberately not re-counted from them: a churn cycle's declared bounds are ceilings for a wedged console rather than intervals a run spends, and 200 of them summed would describe no run this tier has ever performed. The derivation these rows share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`.
